A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ORV and retain identifiable methods, datasets, and results. The complete main papers and appendices are readable, including equations, tables, and figures, supporting reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation experiments on BridgeV2, DROID, and RT-1, conditioning and pretraining ablations, and qualitative analyses in Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 retains original video-generation results and adds visual-planning, policy-learning, conditioning, and robustness experiments in Tables 1–7 and the supplementary material.

M1.justification: The backbone, chunked action modulation, visual-conditioning injection, and multiview architecture are retained. The stated Gaussian rendering specification changes normalized depth from (0,1] to [1,2). The new policy-data augmentation workflow also introduces VLM captioning and quality filtering; expanded explanations of existing action conditioning do not constitute a new architecture.

E1.justification: The original three video datasets remain; naming their curated occupancy data ORV-Data does not itself expand coverage. Substantial new coverage comprises VP2 visual planning using Robosuite and RoboDesk, policy learning evaluated on four SimplerEnv-WidowX tasks, and mismatched coarse/fine conditioning scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds occupancy-conditioned IRASim comparisons and evaluates IRASim on DROID, previously absent. New planning comparisons include MCVD, FitVid, MaskViT, iVideoGPT, and the simulator reference. Policy experiments compare RoboVLM and SpatialVLA training variants, while Table 4 quantitatively evaluates ControlNet-style conditioning.

E3.justification: New protocols include planning training on 5K Robosuite and 35K RoboDesk trajectories, equal-size policy-finetuning datasets with approximately 25% synthetic data, and cross-granularity conditioning tests. Original video preprocessing tables and the 30K-plus-20K training schedule are retained. v2 also explicitly excludes AVID's reported FID from comparison because of an evaluation-mode problem.

E4.justification: Beyond retained depth/semantics and pretraining ablations, v2 tests action-modulation placement, temporal chunking, and ControlNet versus input-noise conditioning in Table 4. It adds quantitative multiview ablation results, coarse/fine transfer tests, and Gaussian-scaling sensitivity examples in Table 6, Table 7, and Figure 12.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without repeated-run information. v2 Table 2 introduces means and standard deviations over three runs for visual planning. Video-generation and policy-learning tables still report point estimates; the PDFs do not establish increased repetition of the retained experiments.

E6.justification: Full-condition ORV scores remain unchanged between v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 1, including BridgeV2 PSNR 28.258 and FVD 16.525. v2 adds comparator, planning, policy, and ablation results. Table 3 reports RoboVLM success increasing from 29.8% to 33.9% and SpatialVLA from 36.2% to 38.5% with augmentation. Table 6's stated with/without ordering conflicts with its claimed improvement, leaving that direction ambiguous.

T1.justification: v2 adds a mathematical state/observation and conditioning formulation in Section 3.1 and a perspective-projection derivation motivating Gaussian scaling in Section 10.1.2. v1 states the scaling rule without this derivation. Existing camera-alignment, condition-fusion, and positional-encoding equations are retained.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes controllable video generation, multiview synthesis, and sim-to-real transfer, presenting downstream learning largely as a prospective benefit. v2's abstract, contributions, and conclusion explicitly claim demonstrated improvements in visual planning and policy learning, substantially extending the claimed contribution beyond video synthesis.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly characterizes ORV as non-interactive and dependent on complete action/occupancy priors, limits demonstrated policy augmentation to appearance changes, and places policy evaluation inside the world model outside scope. Section 12 adds substantive discussion of conditioning robustness, online occupancy forecasting, and long-horizon limitations while retaining the earlier joint-representation and multiview-initialization limitations.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents embedding models, 51 semantic clusters, RAFT filtering, multiview weight initialization, x-flux initialization, VLM prompts/filtering, policy checkpoints, full versus LoRA finetuning, and asset licenses. It also advertises data access alongside code/models. Conversely, v1's batch size 64, learning rate 1e-4, AdamW coefficients, and explicit singleview-module freezing statement are omitted.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion is substantially refocused and expanded through Section 12. Added works include VAP, Ctrl-World, WristWorld, and policy-data synthesis research. Comparisons now address interactive versus non-interactive generation, conditioning granularity, appearance augmentation, and the distinct roles of world models in synthesis and policy evaluation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodology narrative, and discussion are extensively rewritten. Dataset curation moves after model formulation and architecture; multiview and sim-to-real methods become nested subsections. The appendices are reorganized into numbered sections with a contents guide and expanded structured discussions.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the overview diagrams, adds an action-modulation diagram, consolidates qualitative results, restructures the main comparison table by conditioning type, and adds experiment tables and figures. Retained material is also relocated: v1 Figures J–L reappear as v2 Figures 24–26 with identical image content.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's untested downstream-usefulness claims through controlled policy-learning and planning experiments. Matched-conditioning comparisons and new mechanism/robustness tests strengthen validation of the design, while explicit offline-input limitations clarify applicability. These gains outweigh the remaining reporting problems, notably Table 6's contradictory ordering and the removal of useful optimizer and training details.
